main.title: Dead or Alive 3
main.subtitle: A tournament for a new console
main.summary: Dead or Alive 3 is Team Ninja's fighting game released alongside the Xbox in North America on 15 November 2001. Familiar competitors return to a tournament whose story centres on DOATEC's attempt to turn the captured Genra into a weapon. Hitomi joins the cast, bringing another fighting style into the series. The new hardware gives the fighters and their surroundings more detail, but the immediate attraction remains the exchange between two people: attack, anticipate the response and find the opening before the opponent does.

cards.heading: A tournament for a new console
cards.text: Dead or Alive 3 is Team Ninja's fighting game released alongside the Xbox in North America on 15 November 2001. Familiar competitors return to a tournament whose story centres on DOATEC's attempt to turn the captured Genra into a weapon. Hitomi joins the cast, bringing another fighting style into the series. The new hardware gives the fighters and their surroundings more detail, but the immediate attraction remains the exchange between two people: attack, anticipate the response and find the opening before the opponent does.

cards.heading: Read the next move
cards.text: Strikes, throws and defensive holds form the central contest. A hold can answer an anticipated attack, while a throw punishes an opponent who relies on that defence. Movement around the arena gives another way to change the exchange. Falls and dangerous boundaries can carry a fight into another part of a stage, so position matters alongside the next combination. The player learns to recognise the opponent's habits and vary their own choices, turning a short sequence of attacks into a conversation about what might come next.

cards.heading: Learn one command at a time
cards.text: The Exercise option in Sparring presents commands on screen and advances after each successful attempt. It offers a practical way to learn a character without searching a move list between every exchange. Japanese and European editions followed in 2002 with additions and adjustments beyond the original North American release. The game sold more than two million copies worldwide and became one of the Xbox's most successful fighting games. Later backward compatibility kept the original release playable on newer Xbox systems, preserving its particular pace and stage design.

main.title: Project Gotham Racing
main.subtitle: City racing with something to prove
main.summary: Project Gotham Racing is Bizarre Creations' city-racing game for the original Xbox, released with the console in North America on 15 November 2001. Licensed sports cars compete on circuits through London, Tokyo, New York and San Francisco. Its Kudos system gives the driver another target alongside the finishing position: performing well enough to make the journey itself count.

cards.heading: A launch-day drive
cards.text: Project Gotham Racing is Bizarre Creations' city-racing game for the original Xbox, released with the console in North America on 15 November 2001. Licensed sports cars compete on circuits through London, Tokyo, New York and San Francisco. Its Kudos system gives the driver another target alongside the finishing position: performing well enough to make the journey itself count.

cards.heading: Making a manoeuvre count
cards.text: Passing a rival cleanly adds Kudos to a temporary score. Holding a slide through a corner can build it further, and linking manoeuvres earns a bonus. The points still need to be secured: striking a barrier or another car too soon can wipe out the latest effort. A corner therefore offers a choice between protecting a promising run and attempting something more ambitious. The car's speed matters, but so does the space left around it.

cards.heading: Choosing the challenge
cards.text: Kudos Challenge arranges events into levels with different demands. A Hot Lap asks for a quick circuit; other challenges put the emphasis on overtaking or following gates marked by cones. Before starting, the player can make the target harder to increase the possible reward. Bronze medals permit progress, while higher awards encourage another attempt with a better car or a more confident line. Unlockable Jokers can double a single challenge's score, making their timing worth considering.

cards.heading: A city through the windscreen
cards.text: The four cities put familiar landmarks beside the barriers and corners of each course. Their different street layouts give the same car another setting to learn, from broad approaches to tighter sequences of turns. Music also becomes part of the drive: the game offers radio stations and lets players assemble a virtual CD using songs stored on the Xbox hard drive. Choosing what plays through the car's stereo brings the console's music features into the race.

main.title: Halo: Combat Evolved
main.summary: Halo: Combat Evolved is a 2001 first-person shooter game developed by Bungie and published by Microsoft Game Studios.

cards.heading: Halo: Combat Evolved
cards.text: Halo: Combat Evolved is a 2001 first-person shooter game developed by Bungie and published by Microsoft Game Studios. The game was released on November 15, 2001 for the Xbox, with ports to Microsoft Windows and Mac OS X released in 2003. It is the first installment in the Halo franchise. Set in the 26th century, players assume the role of Master Chief, a cybernetically enhanced supersoldier. Accompanied by an artificial intelligence construct named Cortana and the human forces of the United Nations Space Command, players battle against an alien theocracy known as the Covenant while they attempt to uncover the secrets of the eponymous Halo, a ring-shaped artificial world.

cards.heading: From strategy prototype to Xbox launch
cards.text: Development of Halo began in 1997. Initially, it was a real-time strategy game that changed during development into a third-person shooter and finally into a first-person shooter. Microsoft acquired Bungie in 2000, intending for Halo to be a launch title for the upcoming Xbox. Despite having a troubled development, Halo introduced multiple new features not previously seen in first-person shooters, many of which became standard in the genre. The game features a local multiplayer component.

cards.heading: An Xbox success grows into a franchise
cards.text: Halo was a critical and commercial success and is often cited as one of the greatest video games ever made. Particular acclaim was given for its campaign, graphics, soundtrack, and multiplayer, although minor criticism focused on the campaign's level design. More than six million copies were sold worldwide by November 2005, making it the second best-selling Xbox game and spawning a multimedia franchise. A sequel, Halo 2, was released for the Xbox in 2004. A remaster of the game, Halo: Combat Evolved Anniversary, was released for Xbox 360 by 343 Industries in 2011, and was re-released alongside the original multiplayer as part of Halo: The Master Chief Collection in 2014. A remake, Halo: Campaign Evolved, was released on PlayStation 5, Windows, and Xbox Series X/S in 2026.

main.title: Xbox
main.subtitle: The ring world and the connected living room
main.summary: Microsoft's first console arrived with a shooter that helped define its controls and social life.

cards.heading: Halo at the launch
cards.text: Xbox launched in North America on 15 November 2001, with Bungie's Halo: Combat Evolved among its games. Halo moved between open combat spaces and enclosed interiors while building a readable control scheme around the console gamepad.

cards.heading: From linked consoles to Xbox Live
cards.text: Split-screen and linked consoles made groups of people part of the experience. Xbox Live followed later, in 2002, extending the platform's social ambitions through an online service.

sources.title: Microsoft Announces Games for the North American Xbox Launch

features.title: Combat within reach of the hands
features.summary: A shooter offers choices beyond aim.

cards.heading: A designer values immediate decisions
cards.text: Before Halo reached Xbox, designer Jaime Griesemer described a game in which immediate decisions should matter alongside accurate shooting. Adding another strategic objective was not, by itself, enough: movement and small tactical choices had to change an encounter. His early interview describes an intention rather than a complete record of the finished game. It is useful because it places the designer's attention on what happens between shots. The player needs meaningful actions to choose, not only a demanding target to keep under a cursor.

cards.heading: Cooperate before composing a message
cards.text: Griesemer applied that reasoning to cooperation too. Talking about a plan, he argued, was less rewarding than actually carrying it out with another player. He wanted cooperative actions to become natural enough that constant explanation was unnecessary, while still providing communication tools. The same interview treats a substantial single-player game as essential context rather than a practice arena for multiplayer. These priorities connect the moment-to-moment encounter with the world around it. A shared action should be understandable through what people are doing, not only through instructions they exchange.

cards.heading: Separate the hands' jobs
cards.text: The original Xbox manual gives those decisions a physical arrangement. One thumbstick moves the player and the other turns and aims; the triggers separate firing from throwing a grenade. Melee and weapon switching have their own buttons rather than requiring a journey through a long inventory. The arrangement lets an encounter change without making the player change devices or stop controlling the camera. Learning the pad still takes practice. The important relationship is that movement, looking and several kinds of response can remain available together.

cards.heading: Read the pause in a fight
cards.text: Information on the visor gives those responses a rhythm. The manual distinguishes health, which does not return automatically, from a shield that recharges when damage stops. Direction indicators locate incoming fire, and the motion tracker shows movement rather than supplying an all-seeing map of every enemy. Pausing behind cover can therefore restore one resource while leaving another depleted. The screen is not merely reporting a score after the fact: it offers signals for deciding whether to continue, withdraw, search for help or approach from another direction.

main.title: Headhunter
main.subtitle: Jack Wade takes the case
main.summary: Headhunter is Amuze's action adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Europe on 16 November 2001.

cards.heading: Jack Wade takes the case
cards.text: Headhunter is Amuze's action adventure, first released for Dreamcast in Europe on 16 November 2001. The player follows Jack Wade, a bounty hunter in a near-future society where criminal punishment and a trade in human organs have become entwined. His investigation moves between armed confrontations and journeys across the city on a motorcycle. The setting resembles Los Angeles, giving the pursuit a recognisable action-film landscape. Jack's work brings that surface into contact with a harsher system beneath it, while the player's immediate task alternates between navigating the streets and surviving inside its buildings.

cards.heading: Between the gunfight and the street
cards.text: On foot, Jack uses third-person shooting and cover to work through hostile locations. The motorcycle connects those principal areas, changing the pace from cautious movement around enemies to travel through the city. Dreamcast's analogue triggers control acceleration and braking, allowing the player to adjust speed with pressure rather than a simple on-off input. Moving between these activities gives the city a role beyond a menu of missions. Reaching the next investigation becomes part of the action, with another set of controls and another kind of space to learn.

cards.heading: An action film on Dreamcast
cards.text: Richard Jacques composed the score, giving the pursuit a large-scale cinematic accompaniment. The game's electric weapons also belong to its premise: conventional guns have been replaced by technology intended to preserve the bodies of the people being hunted. That detail ties the equipment used in the encounters to the society Jack is investigating. A PlayStation 2 version followed in 2002, bringing the same adventure to another audience. On Dreamcast, its combination of motorcycle travel, shooting and orchestral presentation made it an ambitious late addition to the console's library.

main.title: Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader
main.subtitle: Factor 5 / LucasArts · GameCube
main.summary: Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader is Factor 5 and LucasArts' GameCube flying game, following Luke Skywalker and Wedge Antilles through battles associated with the original film trilogy. Released alongside the console in North America, it turns familiar spacecraft and locations into directly controlled missions. Attacking a target, defending an ally or finding an opening through a larger battle gives each sortie its immediate purpose. The player recognises the spectacle from the films, then has to understand which part of it the current craft is expected to change.

cards.heading: The original trilogy from the cockpit
cards.text: Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader is Factor 5 and LucasArts' GameCube flying game, following Luke Skywalker and Wedge Antilles through battles associated with the original film trilogy. Released alongside the console in North America, it turns familiar spacecraft and locations into directly controlled missions. Attacking a target, defending an ally or finding an opening through a larger battle gives each sortie its immediate purpose. The player recognises the spectacle from the films, then has to understand which part of it the current craft is expected to change.

cards.heading: Give the wingmen a useful task
cards.text: The command cross lets the player give limited instructions to supporting pilots while concentrating on the craft under direct control. Different ships have their own weapons, speed and handling, making the mission's objective important to choosing an approach. Completing a level opens the possibility of returning with other available craft. Hidden upgrades improve eligible ships, adding another reason to inspect the surroundings during a replay. The next useful discovery may be somewhere away from the most obvious line toward the current target.

cards.heading: A medal asks for more than survival
cards.text: Completion time, accuracy, destroyed enemies, protected allies and other measures determine the medal awarded after a mission. Meeting the stronger requirements means learning the operation as a connected sequence rather than simply reaching its conclusion. Chris Hülsbeck's score works with John Williams's familiar themes to support that cinematic scale. Rogue Leader became an early demonstration of the GameCube's capabilities, but its repeated appeal rests on the player finding a clearer, more reliable way through a battle that initially seemed overwhelming.

main.title: FreQuency
main.subtitle: Build the song while moving through it
main.summary: FreQuency is Harmonix's PlayStation 2 rhythm game, released in North America on 20 November 2001. The player travels through an octagonal tunnel whose walls carry the separate parts of a song. Drums, bass, vocals and other layers appear as sequences of notes to perform with the controller. Playing a section correctly brings that musical part into the mix. Instead of treating a complete recording as an untouched backing track, the game asks the player to assemble its sound while moving through the tunnel.

cards.heading: Build the song while moving through it
cards.text: FreQuency is Harmonix's PlayStation 2 rhythm game, released in North America on 20 November 2001. The player travels through an octagonal tunnel whose walls carry the separate parts of a song. Drums, bass, vocals and other layers appear as sequences of notes to perform with the controller. Playing a section correctly brings that musical part into the mix. Instead of treating a complete recording as an untouched backing track, the game asks the player to assemble its sound while moving through the tunnel.

cards.heading: Capture a part and move on
cards.text: Completing two measures of a track without an error captures it, allowing that part to continue automatically until a later section. The player can then rotate to another wall and work on the next instrument. Good play fills the song out; repeated mistakes reduce the energy meter and can end the attempt. The tunnel makes those choices visible as neighbouring lanes, so reading the music also means choosing where to go next. Special items can capture a part immediately or increase the points earned.

cards.heading: From performance to remix
cards.text: The track list draws on different contemporary artists, with recordings edited to fit the game's structure. Remix functions let players rearrange musical elements, extending the idea of controlling a song beyond a scored performance. Multiplayer adds another way to divide attention across its tracks. Directed by Greg LoPiccolo, FreQuency established the musical interaction that Harmonix developed in Amplitude in 2003. Its focus on bringing individual parts into a mix offered an early expression of the studio's interest in making recorded music something people could play together.

main.title: Super Smash Bros. Melee
main.summary: Nintendo characters share a GameCube fighting arena in Super Smash Bros. Melee. Familiar stages, items and modes turn the company’s game worlds into a shared competitive playground.

cards.heading: Nintendo worlds meet on one stage
cards.text: Super Smash Bros. Melee is a 2001 crossover fighting game developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the second installment in the Super Smash Bros. series. It features characters from Nintendo video game franchises such as Mario, The Legend of Zelda, Star Fox, Pokémon, and Donkey Kong among others. The stages and gameplay modes reference or take designs from these franchises as well.

cards.heading: Damage becomes distance
cards.text: Melee includes all playable characters from the first game and also adds characters from additional franchises such as Fire Emblem, of which no games had been released outside Japan at the time, in addition to new stages and gameplay modes. Like other games in the Smash Bros. series, Melee's gameplay system offers an unorthodox approach to the fighting game genre, with a counter that measures damage with increasing percentages, representing the knockback the character will experience, rather than the depleting health bar seen in most fighting games.

cards.heading: A worldwide GameCube audience
cards.text: Melee was first released in Japan on November 21, 2001, in North America on December 3, 2001, in Europe on May 24, 2002, and Australia on May 31, 2002. The game received widespread acclaim from critics, earning praise for its visuals, simple controls, gameplay, and orchestrated soundtrack, as well as several awards and acknowledgments from various publications; it is now considered one of the greatest video games ever made. It achieved strong sales upon its release, becoming the GameCube's best-selling title, with over seven million copies sold by 2008.

cards.heading: Competition beyond the original release
cards.text: Due to its fast-paced gameplay and continuously developing metagame, Melee has been featured in many competitive gaming tournaments, and has garnered a dedicated fan community which has kept its competitive scene alive well beyond the game's original lifespan. It was followed by Super Smash Bros. Brawl for the Wii in 2008.

main.title: Rez
main.summary: Rez is a music rail shooter video game developed by United Game Artists and published by Sega for the Dreamcast and PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Rez is a music rail shooter video game developed by United Game Artists and published by Sega for the Dreamcast and PlayStation 2. It was released in Japan in 2001, followed by releases to the United States and Europe in 2002. The game was ported to Xbox 360 as Rez HD by Q Entertainment and HexaDrive in 2008. A virtual reality-compatible expanded version dubbed Rez Infinite was co-developed and released through 2016 to 2023 by Enhance Games, Resonair and Monstars for PlayStation 4, Windows, Android, Oculus Quest and PlayStation 5.

Following a hacker's journey into a malfunctioning AI system, the game has players controlling their avatar as they shoot down numerous enemies. The gameplay and projectile hits sync with the music and have vibration feedback for different controllers, aiming to create a sense of synesthesia. The narrative is told using little description and no dialogue and includes thematic references to the journey of life and technological singularity.

The game was conceived by Tetsuya Mizuguchi during 1994 and 1995, drawing inspiration from European disco music. Production began in 1999 after United Game Artists finished work on Space Channel 5. The design concept drew from rave culture and classic rail shooters, and level design made extensive use of wire frame graphics inspired by the paintings of Wassily Kandinsky. The music, supervised by Keiichi Sugiyama, featured collaborations with multiple Japanese and European music artists and influenced level designs.

The game met with low sales, but strong critical reception due to its music, gameplay and graphics, though several reviewers faulted a lack of content. It also received several industry award nominations, and has been remembered as one of the Dreamcast's best titles. Rez HD and Rez Infinite have likewise met with praise from journalists. Rez Infinite in particular was hailed for its virtual reality integration and its additional Unreal Engine 4-powered zone Area X, described as the closest people might see to a true sequel. Mizuguchi eventually produced a spiritual successor to Rez at Q Entertainment titled Child of Eden.

cards.heading: A gesture joins the beat
cards.text: Locking onto targets prepares a sequence that is released together, making aiming feel like arranging an accent. Rez connects familiar shooting actions with a musical phrase rather than treating them as separate layers. The player listens for a result that is both successful interaction and contribution to a larger composition.

cards.heading: Building a body from progress
cards.text: The avatar changes form as its condition develops. Against the abstract scenery, those transformations make progress and vulnerability visible, giving the player a recognisable presence within the wireframe world.

features.title: Making a shot part of the arrangement
features.summary: Music is prepared in layers so that shots and explosions can become part of the arrangement.

cards.heading: Music that can be taken apart
cards.text: Adam Freeland's account of making Fear for Rez describes supplying parts that the developers could loop and layer during a level. He also provided sounds for events such as explosions. Musical material had to stay coherent while actions changed its arrangement, linking the composer's work to the way the level would be played.

cards.heading: An action can keep musical time
cards.text: Shots and explosions are timed to work with the track's rhythm and key. A successful action consequently has a musical position as well as a visible result. The sound effects help turn aiming and firing into contributions to the arrangement, making the relationship between input and music central to the shooting mechanics.

cards.heading: Area X was a new experiment
cards.text: For Rez Infinite in 2016, Tetsuya Mizuguchi described Area X as an experiment developed through trying and discarding ideas. It introduced a different visual and playable form while retaining the interest in connected sound and action. Its particle-based world extended the project beyond the appearance of the original 2001 levels.

cards.heading: The return had a team behind it
cards.text: Monstars and Resonair helped bring Area X to life, with Sony's support. Their work joined Mizuguchi's direction in the expanded edition, linking its new presentation to a development team and contemporary hardware. The return to Rez involved creating another playable space alongside revisiting the existing levels.

main.title: Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy
main.summary: Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy is a 2001 platform video game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2 (PS2).

cards.heading: Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy
cards.text: Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy is a 2001 platform video game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2 (PS2). The player controls Jak, who sets out to reverse the transformation of his friend Daxter into an "ottsel", a fictional hybrid of an otter and a weasel. This quest eventually turns into an effort to stop a rogue sage from corrupting the world. The game takes place in a cohesive and non-linear world, allowing the player to freely explore interconnected areas.

cards.heading: GOAL and a seamless world
cards.text: The game was conceived during development of Crash Team Racing (1999), Naughty Dog's final Crash Bandicoot game. Pursuing a new intellectual property, the company envisioned a seamless 3D action-adventure that leveraged the PS2's capabilities. The development team built a new engine using Game Oriented Assembly Lisp (GOAL), a custom language for real-time code changes, and recruited animators from Disney and Nickelodeon. Naughty Dog was acquired by Sony during production, providing financial stability. Public anticipation for the game was high prior to its unveiling at E3 2001, where its title was revealed.

cards.heading: Acclaim and a continuing series
cards.text: Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy was critically acclaimed upon release. Reviewers lauded the game's visuals and technical achievements, particularly its open seamless world devoid of load times, which were said to set a new standard for platformers. Praise also went to its gameplay polish, controls, sound effects, and voice acting. Reactions to the music and difficulty were mixed, and criticisms were directed toward the gameplay's lack of innovation, lack of bosses, simplistic story, and short length. By 2002, the game had sold over one million copies worldwide, and by 2007, it had sold two million copies in the United States alone. It is the first installment in the Jak and Daxter series, with the first sequel, Jak II, being released in 2003. A remastered version was released as part of the Jak and Daxter Collection in 2012, and a limited edition physical version for the PlayStation 4 was released by Limited Run Games in 2019.
